# Nitrates

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Cardiology and angiology > Relevant pharmacology > Nitrates*

[Original Article Link](/library/Wm0Peg)

---

## Summary

Nitrates are a class of medications that increase the release of <u>nitric oxide</u> (NO) in vascular <u>smooth muscle cells</u>, leading to <u>smooth muscle</u> relaxation and subsequent <u>vasodilation</u>. <u>Veins</u> are affected more than <u>arteries</u>, and most therapeutic effects of nitrates result from venous pooling and subsequently decreased <u>preload</u>. Rapid- and short-acting nitrates are primarily used in the symptomatic treatment of acute <u>angina pectoris</u> and <u>hypertensive urgency</u>. Side effects may include <u>headache</u> (nitrate-induced <u>headache</u>), <u>gastroesophageal reflux</u>, and <u>hypotension</u> with <u>syncope</u>. Prior intake of <u>PDE-5 inhibitors</u> significantly increases the risk of <u>hypotension</u>.

---

## Agents and dosages

* Organic nitrates (<u>nitroglycerin</u>, <u>isosorbide dinitrate</u>, and <u>isosorbide mononitrate</u>) require activation by <u>mitochondrial</u> aldehyde reductase, therefore, the onset of action is not immediate.

* <u>Sodium nitroprusside</u> is activated non-enzymatically; therefore the onset of action is immediate

* Oral nitrates undergo extensive <u>first-pass metabolism</u> in the <u>liver</u>.

## Pharmacodynamics

* <u>Exogenous</u> supply of <u>nitric oxide</u> (NO) through nitrate → activation of <u>guanylyl cyclase</u> → ↑ <u>cyclic guanosine monophosphate</u> (<u>cGMP</u>) → activation of <u>protein kinase G</u>

* Increases <u>SERCA</u> activity → ↓ intracellular <u>calcium</u> → ↓ recruitment of contractile units → <u>vasodilation</u>

* Increases <u>myosin light chain phosphatase</u> activity → ↓ <u>phosphorylated</u> <u>myosin</u> → <u>smooth muscle</u> relaxation → <u>vasodilation</u>

* Peripheral <u>vasodilation</u>

* Decreased <u>preload</u> through venous dilation (venous pooling);  → reduces <u>myocardial</u> wall tension → improved <u>myocardial</u> <u>perfusion</u>

* Decreased <u>afterload</u> → reduces contraction effort → ↓ <u>myocardial</u> oxygen demand

* Greater <u>vasodilatory</u> effect on <u>veins</u> than <u>arteries</u> (except for <u>sodium nitroprusside</u>)

* Coronary dilation → improved <u>myocardial</u> <u>perfusion</u> 
* In patients with atherosclerotic <u>CAD</u>, <u>arterioles</u> are already dilated to maximize cardiac blood flow (due to flow-limiting stenosis) → difficult to dilate coronary vessels further → limited effect of nitrates

* <u>Anginal</u> <u>pain</u> relief: ↓ <u>preload</u> through venous pooling → ↓ <u>heart</u> size → ↓ oxygen demand → ↓ <u>pain</u>

## Adverse effects

* Circulatory dysregulation: <u>hypotension</u>, reflex <u>sympathetic</u> activity → <u>reflex tachycardia</u> → nitrate <u>syncope</u> 
* <u>Beta blockers</u> can be applied to counter this mechanism

* Nitrate-induced <u>headache</u> (due to the dilation of the cerebral <u>arteries</u>)

* Flushing

* <u>Gastroesophageal reflux</u> (due to the relaxation of the <u>lower esophageal sphincter</u>)

* Development of tolerance 
* Prevention: intermittent therapy with nitrate-free intervals of at least 8 hours

* <u>Cyanide toxicity</u> after <u>sodium nitroprusside</u> infusion (see <u>cyanide poisoning</u>)

* <u>Methemoglobinemia</u>

* “Monday disease”

* Industrial workers who are exposed to nitrates during the work week develop a tolerance over the course of the week.

* No exposure during weekends leads to loss of tolerance.

* Reexposure on Monday causes <u>dizziness</u>, <u>tachycardia</u>, and <u>headache</u>.




We list the most important adverse effects. The selection is not exhaustive.

---

## Indications

* <u>Angina pectoris</u>

* Short-acting nitrates such as sublingual <u>nitroglycerin</u>, <u>isosorbide dinitrate</u>, or <u>nitroglycerin</u> spray for treatment of acute attacks

* Long-acting nitrates such as <u>isosorbide mononitrate</u> can be taken regularly (2–3 times daily) for <u>anginal</u> prophylaxis: unlike some other nitrates, <u>isosorbide mononitrate</u> does not undergo first-pass metabolism by the <u>liver</u> and thus has ∼100% <u>bioavailability</u>.

* <u>Hypertensive crisis</u>: short-term reduction of blood pressure

* <u>Acute coronary syndrome</u>

* Hypertensive <u>pulmonary edema</u>

* Chronic <u>heart failure</u>





References:[[1]](/library/XC09qR)[[2]](/library/8kaOpk)

---

## Contraindications

* <u>Hypotension</u>
* Risk of life-threatening <u>hypotension</u> if taken within 24 hours of a <u>PDE-5 inhibitor</u> (e.g., patients with <u>angina pectoris</u>)

* Stenosis of the <u>left ventricular</u> ejection tract;  (e.g., <u>aortic stenosis</u>, <u>hypertrophic cardiomyopathy</u>)

* <u>Myocardial infarction</u> with <u>right ventricular failure</u>

* <u>Increased intracranial pressure</u>





References:[[3]](/library/KgYUwo)




We list the most important contraindications. The selection is not exhaustive.
